title: More skills, harder choice
caption: Skills that look alike leave the AI guessing; a short list in the project instructions takes the guess away.
analogy: Near-twin cards leave the pilot guessing; the list on the wall settles it.

hick.title: Hick's law, a finding about people
hick.text: People take longer to choose as the information in the choice grows.
hick.source: Hick 1952, Hyman 1953: choice-reaction experiments in people. That a longer list makes an AI choose worse is an inference, not a measured result.

vercel.title: Vercel's agent evals: pass rate

rows.agents-md-line: + a line in AGENTS.md telling the agent to use its skill

vercel.note: With the line, the skill was opened in 95%+ of cases. One docs skill, one framework. A docs index replacing the skill reached 100%.

naming.rule: Name it as an action, lowercase words joined by hyphens
naming.source: Anthropic's skill-authoring best practices: names use lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only; action-oriented names such as process-pdfs and analyze-spreadsheets are listed as acceptable (the gerund, processing-pdfs, is preferred), and patterns should stay consistent across a collection.

alt.room: The control room. Above the console hangs the skill index, eight cards, four of them near-twins drawn dashed and lighter. The pilot sits at the console under a question mark. On the wall to the right the project brief lists three skills; its first line, Collect sediment sample, is lit, and a line runs from it to that one card in the index.

choosing-among-many-skills-hick-and-hyma.header: Choosing among many skills: Hick and Hyman, a finding about people
choosing-among-many-skills-hick-and-hyma.description: Hick applied information theory to choice-reaction-time experiments with up to ten alternatives [1]. Hyman reports that reaction time rises linearly with the amount of information in the choice [2]. That a longer list makes an AI choose worse is an inference, not a measured result.

hick-rate-of-gain-of-information.title: Hick, On the Rate of Gain of Information (Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1952)

hyman-stimulus-information.title: Hyman, Stimulus Information as a Determinant of Reaction Time (Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1953)

agents-md-index-beat-skills-vercels-test.header: An AGENTS.md index beat skills: Vercel's test
agents-md-index-beat-skills-vercels-test.description: a line in AGENTS.md telling the agent to use its skill raised the pass rate from 53% to 79%, and the skill was opened in 95% or more of cases [1]. A compressed docs index of about 8KB in AGENTS.md, replacing the skill, reached 100%. Vercel's working theory: no decision point, and skills load only when invoked [1]. It is one docs skill for one framework, not a procedure.

vercel-agents-md-outperforms-skills.title: Jude Gao (Vercel), AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals

skills-too-broad-or-too-narrow.header: Skills too broad or too narrow
skills-too-broad-or-too-narrow.description: the standard warns that skills "scoped too broadly become hard to activate precisely", while too narrow forces several to load [1]. No source measures lookalike skills lowering the pick rate directly.

agent-skills-best-practices.title: Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators

name-each-skill-as-an-action.header: Name each skill as an action
name-each-skill-as-an-action.description: Anthropic's skill-authoring best practices say a skill's name uses lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens only, prefer the gerund form (processing-pdfs) and list action-oriented names such as process-pdfs and analyze-spreadsheets as an acceptable alternative; they advise against inconsistent patterns within a skill collection [1]. This Episode names its skills in the action form, collect-sediment-sample.

anthropic-skill-authoring-best-practices.title: Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices (Claude Platform docs)

near-twins.title: Near-twins
near-twins.script: Now see what happens when the skills pile up. "Sample", "Take sample", "Seabed sample v2": three skills whose descriptions sound alike, and a model that has to guess between them. It guesses, and you made it do so.

a-short-list-on-the-wall.title: A short list on the wall
a-short-list-on-the-wall.script: The fix is cheap: a short list in your project instructions, AGENTS.md if you work with a coding agent, that says "In this project, use these three skills." Project instructions are always loaded, so the model no longer has to choose from a crowded index. On our ship, that is a list on the wall.

hicks-law.title: Hick's law
hicks-law.script: People have the same trouble: the more the options look alike, the longer it takes to choose, and psychologists call that Hick's law. I am lending it to the model, so hold it as a picture, not a measurement. What I want you to take from this Slide is the short list: it is short, and it is always loaded.

name-it-as-an-action.title: Name it as an action
name-it-as-an-action.script: One more habit keeps the index tidy: name each skill as an action, in lowercase words joined by hyphens, like collect-sediment-sample. A name that says what the skill does tells the model, and you, what it is for before anyone reads the description, and when every name follows the same pattern, a near-twin stands out before it gets written.
